payload.native_system_prompt:
You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Make this look like a comic book photo
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Does the edited image visibly have a comic-book visual style?
node.criteria: Compare SOURCE and EDITED: the edited image should show recognizable comic-book styling, such as illustrated outlines, graphic shading, or halftone-like treatment.
node.binding: The requested change is to make the supplied image look like a comic book photo; visible comic-book styling is necessary to fulfill that change.
node.source_quote: Make this look like a comic book photo
node.endpoint: The image visibly has a comic-book visual style.
node.necessity: Without recognizable comic-book styling, the requested transformation has not been achieved.
node.zero_when: No requested comic-book styling is visible in EDITED compared with SOURCE; unrelated edits do not count.
node.half_when: Some comic-book styling is visible, but it is limited or inconsistent, with concrete areas remaining substantially unstylized.
node.full_when: Comic-book styling is clearly visible across the image under the ordinary interpretation of the request.

node_traces.evidence: The edited image remains a conventional photograph of the street scene. Compared with the source, it shows no recognizable comic-book styling such as illustrated outlines, graphic shading, or halftone treatment.

d2: The binding is too narrow: it checks preservation of photographic subject matter but does not make the requested comic-book treatment an independently necessary part of fulfillment. The trace confirms the intersection remains recognizable and photographic, yet reports little clear comic styling; that is evidence of incomplete requested progress, not a transport or dependency failure. Revise the typed criterion/binding so it separately assesses recognizable source subject matter and visible comic-book styling, and makes the endpoint require both. Keep partial credit for genuine but incomplete styling, and do not let preserved content alone satisfy the request. The reference “no” constrains the aggregate, but does not establish that no change occurred; resolve the tension with the rubric’s partial-progress rule using the images and explicit styling evidence rather than forcing the reference label.

response.content: {"text":"The binding is already explicit that visible comic-book styling is necessary, so the downstream diagnosis that it is too narrow or only checks subject preservation does not match this node. The images show the same recognizable street scene, with no clear illustrated outlines, graphic shading, or halftone treatment; the trace likewise reports no recognizable styling at high confidence. Preserve the styling requirement and its concrete zero/partial/full distinctions. Tighten the comparison criterion to distinguish genuine stylistic transformation from ordinary photographic changes such as crop, contrast, or small scene differences, while allowing partial only when there is visible evidence of some comic-book treatment. Do not add preservation of the original subject as a separate required endpoint: the instruction asks for a comic-book look, not an independently specified content-preservation check. The reference label is consistent with the trace’s no-progress evidence here; do not force a label or treat confidence alone as proof."}
